title: The hidden life of unicellular red algae: discovery of a common sexual cycle unlocks a model lineage for eukaryotic evolution
content: From land plants to algae, the entire Archaeplastida supergroup traces its lineage back to a primary endosymbiotic event that occurred about 1.5 billion years ago (Yoon et al. 2004). Within this group, the early-branching class of unicellular red algae (Cyanidiophyceae) have become a critical phylogenetic reference, providing essential insights into eukaryotic evolution, especially regarding adaptations in cell morphology, organelle structure, and environmental responses (Bowles et al. 2023). Cyanidiophyceae thrive worldwide in the thermo-acidic environment of hot springs and volcanic areas (pH 0.05 to 5.0, <56 °C) and display one of most compact nuclear genomes among eukaryotes (8.7 to 17.8 Mb, compared to 3.2 Gb for humans and 16.8 Gb for wheat), thereby functioning as a cornerstone for understanding the minimal requirements of eukaryotic life. Since their first description (Galdieri 1899), these organisms were believed to lack a sexual life cycle, solely reproducing asexually. Recently, however, a sexual reproduction process has been identified in Galdieria, 1 of the 8 genera composing this class (Hirooka et al. 2022). Tracking the evolution of such traits necessitates phenotypic and genotypic comparisons, combined with genetic manipulation of model organisms. However, the narrow phylogenetic range of available models constrains research, leaving the evolution of sexual life cycles within the Archaeplastida poorly understood.
